title: Do you prefer using AI with an engine or game framework?
author: Rob_Blob
selftext:
Do you prefer using AI for game development with an established engine (Unity, Godot, ect.) or a game framework (SFML, Love2D, ect.)?

As an experienced SWE who has already learnt a lot about game programming patterns building my own engine from scratch before AI, I suspected pairing AI with a game framework would actually be easier than with an engine, because you could just describe the architecture of your game and its systems, and then have AI build everything out according to your specs. I assumed using an engine would almost add an unnecessary layer of complexity versus letting AI interface directly with the pure source code of a game.

But I would like to hear from the community, especially those who have played around with both workflows. Which do you prefer and why?

comments.author: Dry-Calligrapher-857
comments.body:
Im working with love2d   
Tried godot and using mcp but it gets weird and you have to really know your way around otherwise it start creating weird nodes or stuff you dont really want

comments.author: Dapper-Business5405
comments.body:
I'm using Godot 4 with Claude Code for my game (a small kiosk tycoon), so I can only speak for the engine side. For me the engine was the right choice, and I think there are 2 reasons:

first reason is that I work in the Godot editor myself. When the AI builds something, I can just open the scene, move things around and see the result right away. With a pure framework I would have to ask the AI for every little change.

second reason: Godot is kind of "AI friendly", because the scenes (.tscn) and scripts are plain text files. The AI can read and change them like normal source code, and it can run Godot headless to check for errors after every change. That catches a lot of mistakes before I even start the game.

To be honest, I never would have made a game without AI, so I don't have your background with building an engine from scratch. With your experience, a framework could work really well for you, because you know exactly which architecture you want. I would be curious which way you go 😄

comments.author: sirpalee
comments.body: Code only engine, like bevy works the best with ai coding agents.

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body: Game engine, in my case Unreal Engine. Im already used to it for 3D art purposes and my entire pipeline is optimized to be used with Unreal Engine - from 3ds Max, Maya and Zbrush to Marvelous Designer, Gaea and some other software i use in my pipeline and workflow. When UE6 comes out it will be even better given that the current version of 5.8 is still "only" experimental with AI and MCP.

comments.author: kaliffen79
comments.body:
[https://martinfowler.com/articles/llm-and-dsls.html](https://martinfowler.com/articles/llm-and-dsls.html)

I am currently exploring this technique.  I'm making DSLs for things id like to focus on.  (have depth in).

Then I use agents to build the framework that supports it (could be in any engine or your own)

Say i did a DSL for strategy games, where i could express the states and rules

Now the conversation shifts from building the whole stack to making mechanics.  These can be checked, run with a generic engine, and the development cycle becomes very fast (on this area).

Have you ever asked an half decent LLM to make a mermaid diagram?  they usually nail it.   A small dsl with examples that fit in context makes the agent very focused, since there is a paved path

Con: you have to maintain the dsl.  Thats a pain, but I am leaning towards that the pros outweigh it.

comments.author: lawlshawk
comments.body:
honestly i think engine vs framework matters less than how fast the AI can check its own work

  
i usually target unity but right now im experimenting with three.js + a custom js engine wrapped in tauri. obvious pros and cons with a js framework, i get that ... but it's a single player platformer so i don't need a ton of what an engine gives you. nice part is the game logic is just code so the agent can check its own work pretty fast

  
on the unity side i've had pretty decent results with blender mcp for assets and the unity cli for the engine stuff. engines can get there, it just takes more setup

  
with your background i'd probably lean framework. you already know the architecture you want and AI is pretty good at building to a spec. just budget for the stuff an engine hands you for free like a level editor / asset import ... you'll end up having it build some of that lol

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body:
I think for most developers trying to focus on building a game primarily, you probably want to go with a platform which is opinionated on architecture unless you have good reasons to have your own differing opinions about architecture.

This will unfortunately mean that, if you want to do certain "creative" things, you may have implicately chosen an architecture which makes it more difficult than it has to be to do them performantly.  And likely your AI assistant isn't smart enough to warn you of the impending wall your game dev car is hurtling towards until a massive refactor is required.

The glowing example is voxel games (minecraft procedural world) are a poor fit for any of the big mainstream engines because they're virtually all tuned for a relatively small number of highly complex objects rather than an absurdly high number of simple objects.  It's not impossible to work around this tuning, but if you don't realize the problem before it's too late, and haven't done any "premature optimization" you can end up stuck in traffic with a massive sprawling game codebase that needs a MAAAASIVE refactor before it's anywhere near shippable.

The only real workaround is understanding the technical constraints of the project you're trying to build up front, and designing the architecture early, then understanding how well/poorly that architecture maps onto the various engine and frameworks out there, and what needs to be built early to allow project goals with the platform you ultimately choose.

AI can help tremendously with all these architecture and design substeps, but if you just throw a huge sloppy game design doc at it, and fail to ask the right questions, it will likely overlook the forest for the trees and happily lead you down the path of impending disaster.  AI tends to be quite bad for intuition about how complex systems with multiple competing constraints can be balanced to achieve optimal results in as many categories as possible.  It tends to hyperfocus on one main thing at the expense of all others.

comments.author: random_boss
comments.body:
I just prefer engines, because it comes to the fact that for most systems that engines handle I don’t have a strong sophisticated opinion, so not only am I forced to reinvent wheels engines already solved, but I’m doing at the cost of my tokens that could be going into actually making the game. In the game I have going in a framework right now I’m having to reinvent particle systems and it’s making me want to claw my eyeballs out and die. The agents pick some reasonable defaults but I keep having to be like “no not like that, like this” and then they do it and I have to be like “well, I mean, obviously not like *that*” and it’s all because I didn’t plan on reinventing a particle system, so I had no strong plan about all the ins and outs of how to do, and now I’m forced to confront doing that or this thing about my game will suck. 

Ironically I’ve run into that same problem on my Unity project; I’ve spent the last two weeks reinventing character animation and locomotion system that you get for free in unreal and it makes me want to die. Such a massive fucking waste of effort and tokens when I could just be making the game.

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body:
I built from scratch in Rust. For context I'm making a 2d game and I'm targeting really low level hardware (ARM processors with 2gb ram) so I wanted something that I could optimize the hell out of.

I had also built my own game engine prior to using AI so I think you should at least try it if you haven't already. I think for those of us with existing knowledge about how these systems actually work removing the framework can be nice (I also in general never liked using "established engines").
